mainTopic: Space rights in shared courtyards and alleyways: the four cubits in front of entrances, and neighbors' power to block changes to doors and alleyway use
overview: This amud discusses the space that houses around a shared courtyard or alleyway are entitled to. It opens with the ארבע אמות (four cubits) given in front of an entrance, and the reason for them: room to unload an animal (פירוק משאו). Using that test, רב הונא rules that an אכסדרה gets no four cubits, and the גמרא settles a ברייתא against him by saying it means a Roman portico. A chicken coop and a half-roofed house also get none, since there is no unloading or one can unload inside. רב הונא then asks רבי אמי two questions. Can residents stop a man from moving his door onto their alleyway? Yes. Is the burden of housing soldiers split by people or by doors? By people. רב הונא rules that neighbors can stop someone from building in front of his own door. A ברייתא seems to contradict him, and the גמרא answers that this is a dispute between רבי and רבי שמעון בן אלעזר. Finally, רבא rules that a sealed door may be reopened only if its doorposts were never broken, and אביי begins quoting a ברייתא that supports him, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: A set entrance gets only four cubits in front of it
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא limits the previous ruling. If one specific entrance is set aside, the owner gets only four cubits in front of that entrance.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if he sets aside an entrance for it, he gets only four cubits in front of his entrance.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the ruling from just before this point. It says that once a single entrance is set aside, only the space in front of that entrance counts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without a set entrance, a person might reach the spot from any side and need room all around. Once one entrance is designated, he only uses that side. So he only gets four cubits there.

keyTerms.meaning: sets aside, designates
an entrance, a doorway
four cubits, the space given in front of an entrance

phrases.english: But if he designates an entrance for it,
phrases.notes: This continues the case from just before this amud, which is about a pit in the courtyard.

phrases.english: he has only four cubits
in front of his entrance.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲבָל מְיַיחַד לֵיהּ פִּיתְחָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Qualifies the ruling from the previous section of the daf
steps.mimraCoreRuling: With a designated entrance, only four cubits in front of that entrance are given.

steps.title: A portico gets no four cubits, since one can unload inside
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא rules that an אכסדרה does not get four cubits. The גמרא explains why: the four cubits exist for unloading, and one can unload inside the portico.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא said: A portico does not have four cubits. What is the reason? The four cubits are for unloading his burden. Here he can go inside and unload.
steps.whatsHappening: רב הונא gives a new ruling about a portico. The גמרא then explains it using the basic reason for the four cubits.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The four cubits are given so a person has room to unload his animal outside his door. An אכסדרה is open, so he can bring the animal inside and unload there. No reason means no four cubits.

keyTerms.meaning: a portico, a roofed area open on at least one side
what is the reason?
unloading his burden from the animal
goes inside

steps.whyThisMatters: The test of פירוק משאו set up here is the measuring stick for every case in the rest of this section.

phrases.english: Rav Huna said:
A portico does not have four cubits.
What is the reason?
phrases.notes: He means: why are four cubits given to entrances in the first place?

phrases.english: Because of unloading his burden;
here, it is possible for him to go inside and unload.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב הוּנָא: אַכְסַדְרָה – אֵין לָהּ אַרְבַּע אַמּוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new topic about which structures get four cubits
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An אכסדרה has no four cubits, because one can unload inside it.

steps.title: A ברייתא says porticos do get four cubits
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת quotes a ברייתא that gives four cubits to both house gates and portico gates, which seems to contradict רב הונא.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ששת objected: Both gates of houses and gates of porticos have four cubits!
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת attacks רב הונא with a ברייתא that says the opposite.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב הונא said a portico gets no four cubits. The ברייתא openly lists portico gates as getting them. An אמורא cannot argue with a ברייתא, so רב הונא needs an answer.

keyTerms.meaning: gates of houses

phrases.english: Rav Sheshet raises an objection:
Both gates of houses
and gates of porticos
have four cubits!

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵתִיב רַב שֵׁשֶׁת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב הונא's ruling
steps.kashyaTarget: רב הונא's ruling that an אכסדרה has no four cubits
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא explicitly gives four cubits to portico gates.

steps.title: The ברייתא means the portico of a study hall
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא is about the portico of a בית רב, which is closed and not a place for unloading.
steps.simpleTranslation: When that ברייתא was taught, it was about the portico of a study hall.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב הונא by saying the ברייתא is talking about a different kind of portico.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A study hall's portico is not a place where you would bring an animal and unload. Since you cannot unload inside, it needs the four cubits outside. So there is no contradiction with רב הונא.

keyTerms.meaning: when that ברייתא was taught
a study hall, house of learning

phrases.english: When that was taught,
it was about the portico of a study hall.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי תַּנְיָא הָהִיא, בְּאַכְסַדְרָה דְּבֵי רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב ששת's objection
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the ברייתא to a specific case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא seemed to mean all porticos.
steps.terutzMaskana: It only means a study hall's portico, where one cannot unload.

steps.title: A study hall's portico is obviously a full room
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects that answer. A study hall's portico is a real room, so of course it gets four cubits; the ברייתא would not need to say it.
steps.simpleTranslation: The portico of a study hall is obvious. It is a proper room!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on its own answer. It says the ברייתא would not bother teaching something so obvious.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A closed study hall portico is just like a house. Of course it gets four cubits like any house. The ברייתא's mention of porticos must be teaching something new.

keyTerms.meaning: it is obvious
a proper, full room

phrases.english: The portico of a study hall is obvious;
it is a proper room!

steps.triggerLanguage: אַכְסַדְרָה דְּבֵי רַב פְּשִׁיטָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the answer in step 4
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that the ברייתא refers to a study hall's portico
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: That case is too obvious for the ברייתא to need to teach it.

steps.title: The ברייתא means a Roman portico
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא gives a new answer: the ברייתא is about a Roman portico, a type that is not a full room but still is not used for unloading.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is about a Roman portico.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא replaces its first answer with a better one, and this settles רב ששת's challenge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A Roman portico is more open than a study hall's portico, so it is not obvious that it gets four cubits. But it is also not used for unloading, so it does get them. רב הונא's ruling stands for an ordinary portico, where you can unload inside.

keyTerms.meaning: rather, introducing a new answer
a Roman-style portico

steps.whatToRemember: An ordinary אכסדרה gets no four cubits because you can unload inside. The ברייתא that gives them four cubits is talking about a Roman portico, which is not used for unloading.

phrases.english: Rather, it is about a Roman portico.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא בְּאַכְסַדְרָה רוֹמָיְיֹתַא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a new answer after step 4's answer was rejected
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the ברייתא to a different specific case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא refers to a study hall's portico.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא refers to a Roman portico, which is not used for unloading.

steps.title: Gatehouse, portico and balcony get four cubits; five houses on a balcony share them
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that a gatehouse, a portico and a balcony each get four cubits. If five houses open onto one balcony, together they get only four cubits.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: A gatehouse, a portico and a balcony have four cubits. If five houses open onto a balcony, they have only four cubits.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא listing more structures that get four cubits.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even a balcony gets four cubits, because people come down from it to the courtyard. When many houses open onto one balcony, they all use the same way down. So they share one set of four cubits instead of each getting its own.

keyTerms.meaning: a gatehouse
a balcony, with stairs leading down to the courtyard

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
A gatehouse, a portico, and a balcony
phrases.notes: Here the portico gets four cubits; based on the last step, this would be the kind you cannot unload inside.

phrases.english: have four cubits.
If five houses opened onto the balcony,

phrases.aramaic: אֵין לָהֶן אֶלָּא אַרְבַּע אַמּוֹת בִּלְבַד.
phrases.english: they have only four cubits alone.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: בֵּית שַׁעַר, אַכְסַדְרָה וּמִרְפֶּסֶת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a new ברייתא on the same topic
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A gatehouse, portico and balcony get four cubits; several houses on one balcony share a single four cubits.

steps.title: Does a chicken coop get four cubits?
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן asks רבי ינאי whether a chicken coop gets four cubits.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן asked רבי ינאי: Does a chicken coop have four cubits or not?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן asks a new question. This sets up רבי ינאי's answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A chicken coop is a structure with an entrance, like a house or balcony. The question is whether that alone earns four cubits, or whether the purpose of the four cubits must apply.

keyTerms.meaning: he asked him
a chicken coop

phrases.aramaic: בְּעָא מִינֵּיהּ רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מֵרַבִּי יַנַּאי:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yoḥanan asked Rabbi Yannai:
A chicken coop,
does it have four cubits,
or does it not have four cubits?

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּעָא מִינֵּיהּ רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מֵרַבִּי יַנַּאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about a new structure using the same topic
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a chicken coop gets four cubits

steps.title: No four cubits for a coop: chickens just climb up and down
steps.stepSummary: רבי ינאי answers with the unloading reason. Chickens climb up and down on their own, so no unloading space is needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: What is the reason for four cubits? For unloading his burden. Here, the chickens climb up and climb down.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ינאי answers by going back to the reason for the four cubits and showing it does not apply to a coop.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The four cubits are only for unloading an animal's load. Nobody unloads anything at a chicken coop; the chickens climb up and down by themselves. So a coop gets no four cubits.

keyTerms.meaning: climbs and goes up
climbs and goes down

phrases.english: He said to him:
What is the reason? Because of unloading his burden;
here, it climbs up and climbs down.
phrases.notes: The answer is left unsaid, but it is clear: no unloading, so no four cubits.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: טַעְמָא מַאי – מִשּׁוּם פֵּירוּק מַשָּׂאוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבי יוחנן's question
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A chicken coop gets no four cubits, because there is no unloading there.

steps.title: Does a half-roofed house get four cubits?
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks רב נחמן about a house that is half roofed and half open.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא asked רב נחמן: A house that is half roofed and half not roofed, does it have four cubits or not?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא asks a new question. This sets up רב נחמן's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A house normally gets four cubits. But part of this house is open to the sky, so maybe an animal can be brought into that open part and unloaded there.

keyTerms.meaning: roofed, covered
half of it

phrases.english: Rava asked Rav Naḥman:
A house that is half roofed
and half not roofed,
does it have four cubits,
or does it not have four cubits?

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּעָא מִינֵּיהּ רָבָא מֵרַב נַחְמָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new question built on the same unloading test
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a half-roofed house gets four cubits

steps.title: A half-roofed house gets no four cubits
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן answers that a half-roofed house does not get four cubits.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: It does not have four cubits.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן gives a short, clear answer: no four cubits.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Like רב הונא's portico, this house has room inside where an animal can be unloaded. So the reason for the four cubits does not apply.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אֵין לוֹ אַרְבַּע אַמּוֹת;
phrases.english: He said to him: It does not have four cubits;

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אֵין לוֹ אַרְבַּע אַמּוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבא's question
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A half-roofed house does not get four cubits.

steps.title: No four cubits whether the roof is on the inner or outer half
steps.stepSummary: The answer applies both ways. Clearly when the inner half is roofed one can unload inside, and even when the outer half is roofed one can still go in and unload.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not necessary to say this when the roofing is on the inside, since he can go inside and unload. Rather, even when the roofing is toward the outside, he can go inside and unload.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains how far רב נחמן's answer goes, using a 'not only this, but even that' pattern.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The easy case is when the roof is on the inner half. The newer point is that even when the roof is on the outer half, near the door, the owner can still go inside and unload. Either way, the reason for four cubits is missing.

keyTerms.meaning: it is not necessary to say, the obvious case
its roofing
on the inside
toward the outside

steps.whatToRemember: Every case in this section uses one test: is there a need to unload outside? A portico, a chicken coop and a half-roofed house all get no four cubits, because unloading can happen inside or is not needed at all.
steps.confusionAlert: 'לא מיבעיא' does not mean the first case is in doubt. It means the first case is obvious, and the real point is the 'even' case that follows.

phrases.english: It is not necessary to say when its roofing is on the inside,
since it is possible for him to go inside and unload;
rather, even when its roofing is toward the outside,
it is possible for him to go inside and unload.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא מִבַּעְיָא קֵירוּיוֹ מִלְּגָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains how far רב נחמן's ruling reaches
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A half-roofed house never gets four cubits, whichever half is roofed, because one can always go inside and unload.

steps.title: Can neighbors stop a man from moving his entrance to another alleyway?
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא asks רבי אמי whether the residents of an alleyway can block someone from opening his entrance onto a different alleyway.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא asked רבי אמי: If one person living on an alleyway wants to move his entrance so it opens onto a different alleyway, can the residents of that alleyway stop him, or not?
steps.whatsHappening: A new question begins. רב הונא asks whether alleyway residents have the power to stop a newcomer from opening a door onto their alleyway.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The man already has an entrance on one alleyway and wants to switch it to another. The question is whether the people of that other alleyway can object, or whether he is free to make the change.

keyTerms.meaning: He asked of him (a question put to a teacher)
An alleyway that several courtyards open onto
His entrance or doorway
They can stop him, they can block his plan

phrases.aramaic: בְּעָא מִינֵּיהּ רַב הוּנָא מֵרַבִּי אַמֵּי:
phrases.english: Rav Huna asked of Rabbi Ami:
One of the residents of an alleyway,
who wished to turn his entrance to a different alleyway:
can the residents of the alleyway prevent him,
phrases.notes: He means the people of the new alleyway, the one he wants to open his door onto.

phrases.english: or can they not prevent him?

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּעָא מִינֵּיהּ רַב הוּנָא מֵרַבִּי אַמֵּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new topic about alleyway rights after the discussion of the half-roofed house.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the residents of another alleyway can stop someone from moving his entrance onto their alleyway.

steps.title: Yes, the alleyway residents can stop him
steps.stepSummary: רבי אמי answers that the residents of the alleyway can prevent him from moving his entrance there.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אמי said to him: The residents of the alleyway can stop him.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אמי answers the question: the people of the other alleyway have the right to say no.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Moving a door onto an alleyway is not something one person can decide alone. The residents already there have a say and can block the change. The גמרא here does not spell out the reason.

keyTerms.meaning: The residents of the alleyway

phrases.english: He said to him:
The residents of the alleyway can prevent him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: בְּנֵי מָבוֹי מְעַכְּבִין עָלָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 13.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The residents of the other alleyway can block him from moving his entrance there.

steps.title: How is the burden of housing soldiers shared?
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא asks whether the burden of אכסניא is divided by the number of people or by the number of entrances.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא asked further: When soldiers must be housed (אכסניא), is the burden divided according to the number of people, or according to the number of entrances?
steps.whatsHappening: רב הונא asks a second question to רבי אמי. It is about fairly dividing a shared burden among the residents of a courtyard.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two ways to split the load. You could count people, so a bigger household takes more soldiers. Or you could count entrances, so each door takes an equal share no matter how many people live behind it.

keyTerms.meaning: Billeting, the duty to house the king's soldiers or guests
It is divided or shared out
Entrances or doorways

phrases.english: Billeting: is it divided according to people,
phrases.notes: This is the duty to house soldiers in your home when the king orders it. רב הונא is still the one asking.

phrases.english: or is it divided according to entrances?

steps.triggerLanguage: אַכְסַנְיָא – לְפִי בְּנֵי אָדָם מִתְחַלֶּקֶת, אוֹ לְפִי פְתָחִים מִתְחַלֶּקֶת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second question from the same questioner to the same teacher.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether billeting is divided per person or per entrance.

steps.title: It is divided by the number of people
steps.stepSummary: רבי אמי answers that אכסניא is divided according to the number of people.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אמי said to him: It is divided according to the number of people.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אמי answers: count the people, not the doors.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A household with more people carries more of the billeting burden. The number of entrances a house has does not matter for this.

keyTerms.meaning: According to the number of people

phrases.english: He said to him:
It is divided according to people.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: לְפִי בְּנֵי אָדָם מִתְחַלֶּקֶת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 15.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Billeting is divided according to the number of people.

steps.title: A ברייתא supports the answer: dung by entrances, billeting by people
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that says the same thing: dung in a courtyard is divided by entrances, but billeting is divided by people.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is also taught in a ברייתא: Dung in a courtyard is divided according to entrances. Billeting is divided according to people.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up רבי אמי's answer with a ברייתא that rules the same way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא contrasts two cases. Shared dung (used as fertilizer) is split by entrances, but billeting is split by people. So רבי אמי's answer on billeting matches an earlier teaching.

keyTerms.meaning: It is also taught this way in a ברייתא (a supporting source)
Dung or manure, used as fertilizer
A courtyard shared by several houses

steps.whatToRemember: Billeting is shared by the number of people, while shared courtyard dung is split by the number of entrances.

phrases.english: It is also taught so:
Dung that is in the courtyard is divided according to entrances.
Billeting is according to people.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא נָמֵי הָכִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the answer of step 16 with a ברייתא.
steps.raayaObject: רבי אמי's ruling that billeting is divided by people.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא stating dung is divided by entrances and billeting by people.

steps.title: Neighbors can stop someone from building in front of his own door
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא rules that alleyway residents can stop one of them from closing off the area in front of his entrance, because it makes their path longer.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא said: If one of the residents of an alleyway wants to close off the area in front of his entrance, the residents of the alleyway can stop him, because he makes the way longer for them.
steps.whatsHappening: רב הונא gives a new ruling: a person cannot build on the part of the alleyway right in front of his own door if his neighbors object.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even the stretch of alleyway by his own door is not fully his. If he builds there, the others have to walk around the structure. That extra walking gives them the right to block him.

keyTerms.meaning: To close off or block an area (by building)
Opposite his entrance, the area in front of his door
He makes the way longer for them

steps.confusionAlert: This is a different case from step 13. There he wanted to move his door to another alleyway; here he wants to build in the alleyway right in front of his own door.

phrases.english: Rav Huna said:

phrases.aramaic: אֶחָד מִבְּנֵי מָבוֹי שֶׁבִּקֵּשׁ לִסְתּוֹם כְּנֶגֶד פִּתְחוֹ –
phrases.english: One of the residents of an alleyway who wished to close off the area opposite his entrance:
the residents of the alleyway can prevent him,
because he increases the way for them.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב הוּנָא: אֶחָד מִבְּנֵי מָבוֹי שֶׁבִּקֵּשׁ לִסְתּוֹם כְּנֶגֶד פִּתְחוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new independent ruling by רב הונא on alleyway rights.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Alleyway residents can stop a neighbor from building in front of his own entrance, since it lengthens their path.
steps.whyThisMatters: This ruling becomes the target of the challenge that follows, so the next steps test whether it holds up.

steps.title: A ברייתא about five courtyards on one alleyway
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins a challenge to רב הונא by quoting a ברייתא on how five courtyards along one alleyway share its space.
steps.simpleTranslation: The גמרא raises an objection: Five courtyards open onto an alleyway. All of them use the area by the outermost one, and the outermost uses only its own area. The rest use the area by the second one, and the second uses its own area and also the area by the outermost.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a challenge against רב הונא by quoting a ברייתא. This step sets up the source; the exact problem with רב הונא's ruling will be spelled out next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא explains who may use each stretch of the alleyway. Residents further in walk past the outer courtyards, so they use those stretches too. But each courtyard uses only the stretch by its own door and the stretches closer to the street, not the ones further in. This picture of each courtyard's stretch is what will be used against רב הונא.

keyTerms.meaning: The outermost courtyard, closest to the street
The second courtyard, next to the outermost
They use (a stretch of the alleyway)

phrases.english: They raised an objection:
Five courtyards open onto an alleyway:
all of them use the area with the outermost one,
and the outermost uses only its own area.
And the rest use the area with the second one;
and the second uses its own area
and uses the area with the outermost one.

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵיתִיבִי: חָמֵשׁ חֲצֵרוֹת פְּתוּחוֹת לְמָבוֹי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a challenge to רב הונא's ruling in step 18.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב הונא's ruling that residents can stop a neighbor from building in front of his own entrance.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא sets out which courtyards use each stretch of the alleyway. The גמרא will next show how this division seems to conflict with רב הונא's ruling.

steps.title: The innermost courtyard has a private area
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא ends by saying the innermost courtyard uses its own area alone and also shares every other area. That implies it could close off its private area, against רב הונא.
steps.simpleTranslation: It turns out that the innermost courtyard uses its own area by itself, and also uses the areas of every other courtyard together with them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes quoting the ברייתא it began in step 19. This last line is what creates the challenge to רב הונא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the area in front of the innermost courtyard belongs to it alone, nobody else has rights there. So it should be allowed to close that area off. רב הונא said the other residents can stop him.

keyTerms.meaning: the innermost courtyard, the one at the closed end of the alleyway
uses it for itself, meaning nobody else shares that area
each and every one

phrases.english: It turns out the innermost one uses its own area for itself,
and it uses the areas of each and every one together with them.

steps.triggerLanguage: נִמְצֵאת פְּנִימִית מִשְׁתַּמֶּשֶׁת לְעַצְמָהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the ברייתא quoted in step 19 and draws the conclusion that challenges רב הונא.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב הונא's ruling in step 18 that residents can stop one of them from closing off the area in front of his entrance.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The innermost courtyard has a private area that nobody else uses. So closing it off should not harm anyone, and he should be allowed to do it.

steps.title: It is a dispute between תנאים
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that רב הונא follows רבי שמעון בן אלעזר, who holds that all the courtyards share the whole alleyway. The earlier ברייתא follows רבי.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is a dispute between תנאים. A ברייתא teaches: if a resident of one alleyway wants to move his entrance onto a different alleyway, the residents of that other alleyway can stop him. If there was a sealed entrance there and he wants to reopen it, they cannot stop him. This is רבי's view. רבי שמעון בן אלעזר says: five courtyards that open onto an alleyway all use the whole alleyway together.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב הונא. It shows that another תנא disagrees with the ברייתא that challenged him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי holds that each courtyard's rights are limited to the stretch it needs to walk through, so the innermost has a private area. רבי שמעון בן אלעזר holds that everyone shares the entire alleyway, so nobody may close off any part of it. רב הונא rules like רבי שמעון בן אלעזר.

keyTerms.meaning: it is a dispute between תנאים
they can stop him
sealed, blocked up
to turn his entrance around, moving it to face elsewhere

steps.whyThisMatters: רב הונא's ruling stands, because it rests on רבי שמעון בן אלעזר's view that the whole alleyway is shared.

phrases.english: It is a dispute between תנאים.
As it is taught in a ברייתא: one of the residents of an alleyway
who wanted to move his entrance onto a different alleyway –
the residents of the alleyway can stop him.
phrases.notes: These are the residents of the new alleyway he wants to open onto.

phrases.english: If there was a sealed entrance and he wanted to open it –

phrases.aramaic: אֵין בְּנֵי מָבוֹי מְעַכְּבִין עָלָיו; דִּבְרֵי רַבִּי.
phrases.english: the residents of the alleyway cannot stop him; these are the words of רבי.
רבי שמעון בן אלעזר says:
five courtyards that open onto an alleyway –

phrases.aramaic: כּוּלָּן מִשְׁתַּמְּשׁוֹת בַּמָּבוֹי זוֹ עִם זוֹ.
phrases.english: all of them use the alleyway together with each other.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנָּאֵי הִיא. דְּתַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 20.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Attributing the contradicting source to one side of a תנאים dispute
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא is the only view, so the innermost courtyard has a private area and may close it off.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר holds that all courtyards share the whole alleyway, and רב הונא follows him.

steps.title: Why does this ברייתא mention courtyards?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא is puzzled that רבי שמעון בן אלעזר talks about courtyards, when רבי's part of the ברייתא was about moving entrances.
steps.simpleTranslation: Courtyards: who mentioned them?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא notices that רבי שמעון בן אלעזר's words don't seem to respond to anything רבי said in this ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A disagreement should be about the same topic. רבי spoke about moving and reopening entrances, while רבי שמעון בן אלעזר speaks about sharing among courtyards, so something seems missing.

keyTerms.meaning: who mentioned them? Meaning this topic was never brought up

phrases.english: Courtyards: who mentioned their name?

steps.triggerLanguage: חֲצֵרוֹת מַאן דְּכַר שְׁמַיְיהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the wording of the ברייתא brought in step 21.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why רבי שמעון בן אלעזר speaks about courtyards when רבי never mentioned them.

steps.title: The ברייתא is missing words
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא has a gap. רבי also ruled on five courtyards, saying all use the outermost area and the outermost uses only its own. רבי שמעון בן אלעזר disagrees with that.
steps.simpleTranslation: Words are missing, and this is what it teaches: likewise, five courtyards that open onto an alleyway all use the outermost area, and the outermost courtyard uses only its own area, and so on. This is רבי's view. רבי שמעון בן אלעזר says: five courtyards that open onto an alleyway all use the whole alleyway.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא fills in the missing part of the ברייתא. With that part filled in, רבי שמעון בן אלעזר is clearly answering רבי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the missing words are restored, רבי's view matches the five-courtyards ברייתא from steps 19 and 20. That shows the two תנאים really disagree about how the alleyway is shared.

keyTerms.meaning: it is missing words, so the text needs to be filled in
and this is what it teaches
the outermost courtyard, the one nearest the street

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two ends. The outermost courtyard, nearest the street, gets the least shared space. The innermost courtyard, at the closed end, gets to use everything.
steps.whatToRemember: רבי: each courtyard uses only the stretch it walks through, so the innermost has a private area. רבי שמעון בן אלעזר: everyone shares the whole alleyway, and רב הונא follows this view.

phrases.english: Words are missing, and this is what it teaches:
And likewise, five courtyards that open onto an alleyway –
all of them use the outermost one's area together with it,

phrases.aramaic: וְהַחִיצוֹנָה מִשְׁתַּמֶּשֶׁת לְעַצְמָהּ וְכוּ׳; דִּבְרֵי רַבִּי.
phrases.english: and the outermost one uses only its own area, and so on; these are the words of רבי.
phrases.notes: "And so on" points back to the rest of the five-courtyards ברייתא quoted in steps 19 and 20.

phrases.english: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר says:
five courtyards that open onto an alleyway –
all of them use the whole alleyway.

steps.triggerLanguage: חַסּוֹרֵי מִחַסְּרָא, וְהָכִי קָתָנֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 22.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The ברייתא is missing רבי's ruling on five courtyards. רבי שמעון בן אלעזר is disagreeing with that ruling.

steps.title: רבא: reopening is allowed only if the doorposts remain
steps.stepSummary: רבא limits the rule that one may reopen a sealed entrance. It applies only if the doorposts were never broken. If they were broken, the residents can stop him.
steps.simpleTranslation: The master said: if there was a sealed entrance and he wanted to open it, the residents of the alleyway cannot stop him. רבא said: this was taught only when he did not break its doorposts. But if he broke its doorposts, the residents of the alleyway can stop him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to a detail of the ברייתא from step 21, and רבא adds a limit to it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: While the doorposts are still standing, the old entrance still exists, so reopening it is not something new. If the doorposts were broken, the entrance is gone completely. Opening it again counts as a new entrance, which the other residents can block.

keyTerms.meaning: they taught this only in the case of, a limiting formula
its doorposts, the frame of the entrance
broke down, tore out

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר מָר: הָיָה סָתוּם וּבִקֵּשׁ לְפוֹתְחוֹ –
phrases.english: The master said: if there was a sealed entrance and he wanted to open it –
the residents of the alleyway cannot stop him.
רבא said: they taught this only
when he did not break down its doorposts,
but if he broke down its doorposts –
the residents of the alleyway can stop him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר מָר: הָיָה סָתוּם וּבִקֵּשׁ לְפוֹתְחוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to a line of the ברייתא in step 21 and qualifies it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A sealed entrance may be reopened only if its doorposts remain. If the doorposts were broken, the residents of the other alleyway can prevent it.

steps.title: אביי offers support for רבא
steps.stepSummary: אביי tells רבא that a ברייתא supports his ruling. The ברייתא itself comes on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to רבא: a ברייתא is taught that supports you:
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. אביי announces that he has a source backing רבא, and the גמרא quotes it at the start of the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nothing new is ruled here yet. The line opens a proof for רבא's doorpost distinction from step 24.

keyTerms.meaning: a ברייתא is taught that supports you

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ אַבָּיֵי לְרָבָא, תַּנְיָא דִּמְסַיַּיע לָךְ:
phrases.english: אביי said to רבא: a ברייתא is taught that supports you:

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ אַבָּיֵי לְרָבָא, תַּנְיָא דִּמְסַיַּיע לָךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Introduces a proof for רבא's ruling in step 24.
steps.raayaObject: רבא's ruling that breaking the doorposts lets the residents block a reopening.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא that is quoted at the start of the next amud.
